q: According to the Gospels, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up a mountain, where his face shone like the sun and his clothes became dazzling white. Moses and Elijah appeared, and a voice from a cloud declared him the beloved Son. For 10 points, name this event, commemorated on August 6 in many churches.

Fra Angelico painted a famous fresco of this event in a Florentine convent, showing an angel kneeling before a seated woman. In Luke's Gospel, the angel Gabriel tells Mary that she will conceive and bear a son. For 10 points, name this event that is celebrated on March 25.

The Acts of the Apostles says that forty days after Easter, Jesus was lifted up into a cloud while his disciples watched, and two men in white told them he would return. Many churches celebrate this event on a Thursday. For 10 points, name this departure of Jesus to heaven.

Pope Pius IX proclaimed this doctrine in 1854 in the document Ineffabilis Deus. It holds that Mary was kept free from original sin from the first moment of her existence. It is often mistaken for the doctrine of the virgin birth. For 10 points, name this Catholic dogma.

Under Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic monarchs of Spain, a tribunal of this name was established in 1478 to investigate converts suspected of secretly practicing Judaism or Islam. Tomas de Torquemada was its first Grand Inquisitor. For 10 points, give the name of this feared institution.

This sixth-century Italian monk founded a monastery at Monte Cassino and wrote a Rule for the monks that stressed prayer, work, and obedience. His twin sister was Scholastica. Monks following the Rule are known by his name. For 10 points, name this saint, the founder of Western monasticism.

This Basque nobleman was wounded by a cannonball at Pamplona in 1521, and while recovering he read about the lives of the saints. He wrote the Spiritual Exercises and founded the Society of Jesus in 1534. For 10 points, name this saint, the first superior general of the Jesuits.

George Fox founded this Christian movement in seventeenth-century England. Its members believe that each person can receive guidance from an inner light and worship in silence until someone feels moved to speak. William Penn founded Pennsylvania as a haven for them. For 10 points, name this group, formally called the Religious Society of Friends.

This man from Palmyra, New York, said the angel Moroni led him to golden plates that he translated as the Book of Mormon. He founded the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in 1830 and was killed by a mob in Carthage, Illinois. For 10 points, name this founder of Mormonism.

This Christian movement grew out of the Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles in 1906. Its members stress experiences of the Holy Spirit, including speaking in tongues and divine healing. The Assemblies of God belongs to it. For 10 points, name this movement named for the biblical event that happened fifty days after Easter.

First issued in 1549, this book set out English-language services for Anglican worship, replacing Latin liturgies. An Archbishop of Canterbury who was later burned at the stake under Queen Mary was its main author. For 10 points, name this foundational book of the Church of England.

Built in the sixth century under the emperor Justinian, this domed church in Constantinople was the largest cathedral in the world for centuries. It was converted into a mosque after the Ottoman conquest in 1453. For 10 points, name this building, whose name means holy wisdom.

The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 formally used this term for the Catholic belief that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the body and blood of Christ while their outward appearance stays the same. Saint Thomas Aquinas defended it using Aristotle's ideas of substance and accident. For 10 points, give this doctrine.

The Synod of Dort rejected the arguments of Jacobus Arminius over this doctrine, which holds that God has chosen in advance who will be saved. It is associated with Augustine and with the Reformed tradition of John Calvin and the Westminster Confession. For 10 points, name this theological idea.

Augustine developed this doctrine, which holds that Adam and Eve's disobedience in the Garden of Eden left all humans with a sinful nature. Baptism of infants was understood in this context. Orthodox Christians do not accept it in the same form as the Western church. For 10 points, name this doctrine.

Born Karol Wojtyla in Poland, this man became pope in 1978 and was the first non-Italian pope in over 450 years. He survived an assassination attempt in 1981 in Saint Peter's Square. He visited his homeland in 1979, and he was canonized in 2014. For 10 points, name this pope.

This Archbishop of Canterbury was killed by four knights in his cathedral in 1170 after a quarrel with King Henry II. The king reportedly asked who would rid him of a turbulent priest. Pilgrims in Chaucer's tale travel to his shrine. For 10 points, name this man, later declared a saint.

q: Born in Cordoba in 1138, this scholar fled to Egypt and served as a physician while writing his major works. He compiled the Mishneh Torah, a fourteen-volume code of Jewish law. His Guide for the Perplexed tried to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with the Torah. For 10 points, name this medieval rabbi, also known as the Rambam.

This first-century BCE sage, born in Babylonia, led a school that often disagreed with the school of Shammai. Asked to explain the whole Torah while standing on one foot, he reportedly said that what is hateful to you, you should not do to your neighbor. For 10 points, name this rabbi, known as the Elder.

This eleventh-century rabbi from Troyes, France, wrote a verse-by-verse commentary on the Torah and on nearly the entire Talmud. His explanations of difficult words are printed beside the text in standard editions. For 10 points, name this scholar, whose name is an acronym of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki.

Compiled around 200 CE by Judah the Prince, this work organizes the oral law into six orders, such as Seeds, Festivals, and Women. It forms the earliest layer of the Talmud. A tractate called Pirkei Avot, the Sayings of the Fathers, is included in it. For 10 points, name this first major written collection of Jewish oral law.

This word names a form of rabbinic literature that explains and expands on scripture through stories, sermons, and legal reasoning. Collections include Genesis Rabbah and Exodus Rabbah. For 10 points, give this Hebrew term for interpretive commentary on the Bible.

This mystical tradition uses a diagram of ten emanations called the sefirot to describe how an infinite God, the Ein Sof, relates to the world. Its main text is the Zohar, and the sixteenth-century teacher Isaac Luria taught in Safed. For 10 points, name this school of Jewish mysticism.

This movement was founded in eighteenth-century Eastern Europe by the Baal Shem Tov. It stresses joyful prayer, song, and dance, and many of its followers gather around a spiritual leader called a rebbe. Chabad-Lubavitch is a large branch of it. For 10 points, name this revival movement.

This movement, called the Jewish Enlightenment, began in eighteenth-century Germany and encouraged Jews to study secular subjects and join European society. Its leading figure was the philosopher Moses Mendelssohn, who translated the Torah into German. For 10 points, name this movement.

This Viennese journalist was shaken by the Dreyfus affair and wrote The Jewish State in 1896. He organized the first Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897. For 10 points, name this founder of modern political Zionism.

A Bedouin shepherd found the first of these manuscripts in 1947 in caves near Qumran on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea. They include a nearly complete scroll of the book of Isaiah and fragments of nearly every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. For 10 points, name this collection of ancient Jewish texts.

Mattathias started a revolt in Modein against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV in 167 BCE. His son Judah led it, and a priestly dynasty called the Hasmoneans emerged. For 10 points, name this family of Jewish rebels, whose revolt is the basis of Hanukkah.

In 586 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Solomon's Temple and deported leading citizens of Judah to Mesopotamia. Psalm 137 begins By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept. For 10 points, give this term for the forced stay of the Jews in Mesopotamia that ended after the Persian conquest.

The Persian king who conquered Babylon in 539 BCE let the exiled Jews return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple. The Book of Isaiah calls him the Lord's anointed. A clay barrel inscribed with his decree is on display in the British Museum. For 10 points, name this Persian ruler, founder of the Achaemenid Empire.

This first-century historian was a Jewish commander in Galilee who surrendered to the Romans during the siege of Jotapata. He took the name of Vespasian's family and wrote The Jewish War and Antiquities of the Jews. For 10 points, name this Jewish chronicler of the revolt against Rome.

Herod the Great built palaces on this isolated rock plateau overlooking the Dead Sea. About 960 Jewish rebels are said to have died there in 73 CE rather than surrender to the Roman army, which had built a huge siege ramp. For 10 points, name this fortress, a symbol of Jewish resistance.

This term refers to Jews descended from communities of Spain and Portugal. After their expulsion in 1492, many settled in the Ottoman Empire and North Africa, where they spoke Ladino. For 10 points, name this group of Jews, as distinct from the Ashkenazim.

This Germanic language, written in Hebrew letters, was the everyday speech of Ashkenazi Jews in Eastern Europe. Sholem Aleichem wrote the stories that became Fiddler on the Roof in it, and Isaac Bashevis Singer won a Nobel Prize for work written in it. For 10 points, name this language.

This prayer, from Deuteronomy, begins with the words Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. Observant Jews recite it morning and evening, and it is written on the scrolls inside the doorposts of homes. For 10 points, name this central declaration of Jewish faith.

This Aramaic prayer praises the greatness of God and makes no mention of death. Mourners recite it in the presence of a minyan, a quorum of ten, for eleven months after the death of a close relative. For 10 points, name this prayer, the mourner's one.

Jews fast for twenty-five hours on this day, the ninth of the month of Av, to mourn the destruction of the First and Second Temples. Many sit on the floor and read the Book of Lamentations. For 10 points, name this solemn day of mourning.

This holiday, the Feast of Weeks, falls seven weeks after Passover and recalls the giving of the Torah on Mount Sinai. Many Jews stay up all night studying, eat dairy foods, and read the Book of Ruth. For 10 points, name this holiday that also marks the wheat harvest.

On this day, Jews complete the annual cycle of Torah readings and immediately begin Genesis again. Congregants dance seven circuits with the scrolls. It follows the festival of Sukkot. For 10 points, name this holiday whose name means rejoicing of the Torah.

This gold-covered acacia wood chest had two winged cherubim on its lid and held the tablets of the law. The Philistines captured it in battle but returned it, and David brought it to Jerusalem. Uzzah died after touching it. For 10 points, name this sacred container of the Israelites.

While Moses was on Mount Sinai, the Israelites became impatient and asked Aaron to make a god for them. Aaron collected their gold earrings and fashioned this idol. Moses broke the tablets in anger. For 10 points, name this idol, a symbol of idolatry.

This council of seventy-one sages sat as the highest court and legislature of Jewish people in the Second Temple period. The Gospels say its members tried Jesus. It met in the Chamber of Hewn Stone in the Temple. For 10 points, name this ancient assembly.

This Jewish group of the Second Temple period believed in an oral law alongside the written Torah and in resurrection of the dead. They were rivals of the Sadducees, and their teachings became the basis of rabbinic Judaism. For 10 points, name this sect, whose name means separated ones.

This Jewish revolt against Roman rule from 132 to 135 CE was led by a man hailed by Rabbi Akiva as the Messiah. It ended with the fall of the fortress at Betar. The emperor Hadrian afterward renamed Judea. For 10 points, name this uprising, named for its leader.

In this Genesis story, people on the plain of Shinar try to build a city and a tall structure to reach heaven. God confuses their language so that they cannot understand one another. For 10 points, name this story that explains the origin of different languages.

This man, the son of Nun, succeeded Moses and led the Israelites across the Jordan. In the battle of Jericho, the walls fell after priests marched around the city carrying trumpets for seven days. For 10 points, name this biblical leader, who has a book named for him.

The speaker of this book, called Kohelet, repeats that everything is vanity, a chasing after wind. It includes the poem that says there is a time for every purpose under heaven, including a time to be born and a time to die. Jews read it during Sukkot. For 10 points, name this book of Writings, traditionally attributed to Solomon.

q: This process occurs in the cytoplasm and splits a six-carbon sugar into two molecules of pyruvate. It uses two ATP in an investment phase and yields a net gain of two ATP and two NADH. It does not require oxygen, and it is the first stage of cellular respiration. For 10 points, name this metabolic pathway.

The Hershey-Chase experiment of 1952 used radioactive sulfur and radioactive phosphorus to label the proteins and DNA of this kind of virus. After it infected Escherichia coli, only the radioactive phosphorus entered the host cells. This showed that DNA is the genetic material. For 10 points, name this type of virus that infects bacteria.

This enzyme uses a template of RNA to synthesize a strand of DNA. It is carried by viruses such as HIV, which is a member of the Retroviridae. Howard Temin and David Baltimore shared a Nobel Prize for discovering it. For 10 points, name this enzyme that reverses the usual direction of the central dogma.

In 1961, Francois Jacob and Jacques Monod described this genetic unit in E. coli. It consists of a promoter, an operator, and structural genes, and a repressor protein can bind to the operator. The lac one is turned on by lactose. For 10 points, name this cluster of genes controlled together.

This cycle, named for an American biochemist, takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast. The enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, and ATP and NADPH from the light reactions drive the reduction steps. For 10 points, name this light-independent set of reactions that makes sugar.

This process produces ATP when protons flow through the enzyme ATP synthase down a gradient across a membrane. Peter Mitchell proposed it in his chemiosmotic theory and won a Nobel Prize in 1978. For 10 points, name this process that couples an electron transport chain to ATP production.

This is the term for the process in which a cell engulfs large particles or whole microbes by wrapping its membrane around them to form a vesicle. Macrophages use it to destroy bacteria. For 10 points, name this form of endocytosis whose name means "cell eating."

This molecule is the main energy currency of the cell. It consists of adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups, and energy is released when its terminal phosphate bond is hydrolyzed. For 10 points, name this nucleotide abbreviated with three letters.

These cells transmit electrical impulses along an axon and receive signals through branching dendrites. The gap between two of them is called a synapse, where neurotransmitters are released. For 10 points, name these cells that make up the nervous system.

In 1952 Rosalind Franklin took Photo 51, an X-ray diffraction image that led Watson and Crick to this conclusion about DNA. Their model showed two antiparallel strands wound around each other. For 10 points, give this shape of DNA.

A project completed in 2003 found about 20,000 protein-coding genes in humans, spread over 23 pairs of chromosomes. This term names what that project sequenced: the complete set of an organism's DNA. Bacteria, yeast, and fruit flies have also had theirs sequenced. For 10 points, give this term for an organism's entire collection of genetic material.

Plants that live in dry places use this type of photosynthesis, in which stomata open at night to take in carbon dioxide. It is used by cacti and succulents. For 10 points, name this pathway abbreviated CAM.

This hormone is made by the beta cells of the pancreas and lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up sugar. A lack of it or resistance to it causes diabetes mellitus. For 10 points, name this hormone.

This is the name for the process in which genes' relative frequencies in a population change by random chance, especially in small populations. The bottleneck effect and founder effect are examples. For 10 points, give this term.

This type of tissue in plants, found at root tips and shoot tips, is made of undifferentiated cells that divide. Growth in length comes from it. For 10 points, name this plant tissue whose name means "divisible."

This scientist's two laws of inheritance are called the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment. He published results from experiments on pea plants in 1866. For 10 points, name this Austrian friar.

This is the term for the offspring of a cross between parents differing in one trait, such as Tt from TT and tt. They show the dominant phenotype in complete dominance. For 10 points, name this genetic condition of having two different alleles.

This type of natural selection favors both extreme phenotypes over the intermediate one, which can split a population in two. Finches with very large or very small beaks are an example. For 10 points, name this type of selection that can lead to speciation.

These are the structures made of microtubules that pull chromosomes apart during cell division. They attach to centromeres at the kinetochore. For 10 points, name these fibers that form between the two centrioles.

This is the name for the kind of mutation in which one nucleotide is replaced by another, such as the one causing sickle cell anemia. The change can alter a single amino acid in hemoglobin. For 10 points, name this type of small mutation.

This is the term for the maintenance of a stable internal environment in an organism, as in the regulation of body temperature by sweating and shivering. Negative feedback loops regulate it. For 10 points, name this process.

This is the name for the group of organisms of the same species that live in the same area. Ecologists study their size, density, and growth. For 10 points, name this group, which is smaller than a community.

This is the name for the process by which a cell makes proteins from the code on messenger RNA at a ribosome. Transfer RNAs bring amino acids that match each codon. For 10 points, name this step that follows transcription.

This organ of the digestive system produces bile and is the largest internal organ. Bile helps to emulsify fats. For 10 points, name this organ that sits under the diaphragm on the right side of the abdomen.

This tough, rigid layer lies outside the cell membrane of plants, fungi, and bacteria. In plants it is built from cellulose, and in fungi from chitin. For 10 points, name this protective outer layer that gives these cells their shape.

Cells use this process to make ATP when oxygen is available. It breaks down glucose into carbon dioxide and water in the mitochondria. For 10 points, name this process, the reverse in some ways of photosynthesis.

This is the term for a trait that is hidden when a dominant allele is present. A person must inherit two copies of the allele to show it, as in cystic fibrosis. For 10 points, name this kind of allele or trait.

These are the cells that carry out the immune response, including B cells and T cells. They are produced in the bone marrow and are also called leukocytes. For 10 points, name these blood cells that fight infection.

This is the process by which green plants release water vapor through tiny pores on leaves, which are also the sites of gas exchange. For 10 points, name these pores, each surrounded by two guard cells.

This is the name for the type of cells that can develop into many different types of specialized cells. Embryonic ones can become any cell type in the body. For 10 points, name these undifferentiated cells.

q: This principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, the system shifts to counteract the change. It explains why adding more nitrogen to the Haber process pushes the reaction toward more product. For 10 points, name this principle, named for a French chemist.

In 1909, Ernest Rutherford's students Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin foil of this metal. Most passed straight through, but a few bounced back, which showed that the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. For 10 points, name this metal used in the experiment, a precious metal with symbol Au.

This quantity is symbolized by the letter S and measures the disorder or randomness of a system. The second law of thermodynamics says that it of the universe always increases in spontaneous processes. For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity.

This type of reaction forms a new bond when a nucleophile attacks a carbon atom bearing a leaving group. It can proceed by a one-step mechanism with backside attack that inverts the configuration, called SN2. For 10 points, name this kind of organic reaction, where one group takes the place of another.

This theory predicts molecular shapes by assuming that electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and spread as far apart as possible. It predicts that methane is tetrahedral and water is bent. For 10 points, name this model abbreviated with five letters.

This rule says that electrons fill orbitals of the same energy singly, with parallel spins, before any orbital gets a second electron. It is named for a German physicist and explains why nitrogen has three unpaired 2p electrons. For 10 points, name this rule.

This is the name for the chemical reaction between an acid and an alcohol that forms an ester and water. Many fruits and perfumes get their smells from products of it. For 10 points, name this type of reaction.

The Haber-Bosch process uses an iron catalyst at high temperature and pressure to combine hydrogen and nitrogen to make this compound. Fritz Haber won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918 for developing the synthesis. For 10 points, name this compound with formula NH3 that is used in fertilizer.

This is the term for the concentration of a solution measured as moles of solute per liter of solution. A two-molar solution of NaCl has two moles of salt in each liter. For 10 points, give this term, abbreviated M.

This is the term for a laboratory technique in which a solution of known concentration is slowly added from a burette to a solution of unknown concentration until the endpoint is reached. Indicators like phenolphthalein show the color change. For 10 points, name this technique.

This property is a measure of how strongly an atom attracts shared electrons in a bond. Linus Pauling devised a scale for it on which fluorine is the highest at 4.0. For 10 points, name this periodic trend.

This law states that the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature when pressure is constant. It is named for a French physicist who studied hot-air balloons. For 10 points, name this gas law.

In this type of reaction, a species loses electrons. The mnemonic "LEO says GER" tells chemists that "loss of electrons" is this process. For 10 points, name this half-reaction, which always occurs together with reduction.
This equation, written as PV equals nRT, relates the pressure, volume, amount, and temperature of a gas. R is the gas constant. For 10 points, name this equation for an idealized gas.

These compounds contain a carbon-carbon double bond and have the general formula C n H 2n. Ethene is the simplest one, and it is used to make polyethylene. For 10 points, name this family of hydrocarbons.

This is the name for a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base. For 10 points, name this kind of solution, such as one found in blood.

The elements in this block of the periodic table are known as "transition elements" and include iron, copper, and zinc. They often form colored compounds and have multiple oxidation states. For 10 points, name these elements located in the middle groups of the table.

This is the term for the reactant that is completely used up first in a chemical reaction, and it determines the maximum amount of product. For 10 points, name this reactant, whose name includes the idea of a restriction.
This type of radioactive decay emits a particle made of two protons and two neutrons, identical to a helium-4 nucleus. It reduces the atomic number by two. For 10 points, name this decay.

This is the term for the time required for half of a sample of a radioactive isotope to decay. Carbon-14 has a value of about 5,730 years, which makes it useful for dating organic remains. Uranium-238 has a far longer one. For 10 points, name this quantity.

This is the name for the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a neutral gaseous atom. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group. For 10 points, name this periodic trend.

This type of substance conducts electricity when dissolved in water because it breaks into ions. Table salt and strong acids are common examples, and sports drinks are named for them. For 10 points, name this kind of substance.
This is the name for the family of hydrocarbons with only single bonds. Methane, ethane, and propane are the first three members of it. For 10 points, name this family, also called the paraffins.

This is the name for the type of reaction in which a compound breaks into simpler substances, such as water into hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis. For 10 points, name this kind of reaction, the opposite of synthesis.

This is the name for the elements that are shiny, conduct heat and electricity, and are malleable. They are found on the left side of the periodic table. For 10 points, name this class of elements, which includes copper and sodium.

This Frenchman carefully weighed reactants and products in sealed vessels and showed that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. He also named oxygen and hydrogen and showed that combustion involves oxygen. For 10 points, name this scientist, often called the father of modern chemistry.

This is the term for how many grams of a substance are in one mole of it. For carbon-12 it is 12 grams. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is numerically equal to the atomic mass on the periodic table.
This is the name of the type of mixture that has visibly different parts, such as sand and water or a salad. For 10 points, name this type of mixture, which is the opposite of homogeneous.

These are the horizontal rows of the periodic table, numbered 1 through 7. Elements in the same one have the same number of electron shells, and atomic radius generally shrinks across one. For 10 points, name these rows, contrasted with groups.

When two clear solutions are mixed and a cloudy solid suddenly appears, a reaction of this type has occurred. The solid that settles out is also called by this term. Mixing silver nitrate with sodium chloride produces white silver chloride this way. For 10 points, name this kind of reaction in which an insoluble solid forms from solution.

q: Answer these questions about the history of chemistry.

What name is given to the speed at which reactants are converted to products?
What term names a reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants?

q: This process occurs at a convergent boundary where a dense oceanic plate slides beneath another plate and sinks into the mantle. It creates deep ocean trenches and a chain of volcanoes on the overriding plate, as in the Andes and the Cascades. For 10 points, name this process.

This Scottish geologist, called the father of modern geology, noted in 1788 at Siccar Point that tilted rock layers lie beneath flat ones. He argued that Earth is extremely old and that the processes seen today also shaped the past. For 10 points, name this author of Theory of the Earth.

This is the term for a rock-forming idea stating that in an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary layers, the oldest layers are at the bottom and the youngest are at the top. Nicolas Steno proposed it. For 10 points, name this law used in relative dating.

Harry Hess proposed this process at mid-ocean ridges. As magma rises and cools, new crust is added, and the magnetic stripes on either side of the ridge are symmetrical mirror images. It explains why the youngest ocean crust is at the ridge crest. For 10 points, name this process, in which the ocean floor grows outward from the middle of the Atlantic.

This type of fault, such as the San Andreas in California, forms where plates slide horizontally past each other. The motion is called strike-slip, and no crust is created or destroyed. For 10 points, name this type of plate boundary.

This is the name of the effect, caused by Earth's rotation, that deflects moving air and ocean currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. It makes hurricanes spin. For 10 points, name this effect named for a French mathematician.

This is the name of the mass extinction about 252 million years ago that ended the Permian period. It wiped out roughly 90 percent of marine species, including the trilobites. For 10 points, name this event, nicknamed "the Great Dying."

This is the name of the narrow, fast-flowing bands of air in the upper troposphere that blow from west to east. They steer storm systems and are strongest in winter. For 10 points, name these high-altitude winds.

This is the name of a periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean that disrupts weather worldwide. Its name is Spanish for "the boy." For 10 points, name this climate pattern, the opposite phase of La Nina.

This is the name for a place where a plume of hot mantle material rises through a plate and produces volcanoes, such as those that formed the Hawaiian Islands. The plate moves over it, creating a chain of islands. For 10 points, name this feature.

This is the name for the underground layer of porous rock or sediment that holds groundwater and can be tapped by wells. The top of the saturated zone above it is the water table. For 10 points, name this layer, such as the Ogallala.

This type of seismic wave arrives second after an earthquake and moves the ground side to side or up and down. It cannot travel through liquids, which helped scientists show that Earth's outer core is liquid. For 10 points, name this wave, designated S.

This German scientist proposed in 1912 that the continents once formed a single landmass and have since drifted apart. He cited the fit of South America and Africa and similar fossils across oceans. For 10 points, name this man whose theory was later supported by plate tectonics.

This is the term for a gas in the atmosphere, including water vapor, carbon dioxide, and methane, that traps heat and warms the planet. For 10 points, name this kind of gas, which gives its name to an effect.

This is the name for the fraction of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects back to space. Fresh snow and ice have a high value of it, while dark ocean water and forests have a low value. Melting ice lowers it, which speeds warming. For 10 points, give this term.

This is the term for a ridge or pile of unsorted rock and sediment deposited by a glacier at its sides or end. Cape Cod and Long Island were formed from them. For 10 points, name this glacial landform.

This scale ranks hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5 based on their maximum sustained wind speed. It is named for a civil engineer and a meteorologist who was director of the National Hurricane Center. A Category 3 or higher storm is called a major hurricane. For 10 points, name this scale.

This is the name of the large fan-shaped landform of sediment that forms where a river meets a body of standing water. The Mississippi and the Nile each have a famous one. For 10 points, name this landform.

This is the name of the geologic period that started about 541 million years ago and saw a rapid diversification of animal life. Trilobites flourished during it. For 10 points, name this first period of the Paleozoic era.

This is the term for the temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapor begins to condense into liquid. For 10 points, name this temperature, which is also the temperature at which dew forms.
This is the name for the continuous circulation of rock between igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic types through melting, cooling, weathering, and pressure. For 10 points, name this cycle.

This is the name of a violently rotating column of air that extends from a thunderstorm to the ground. It is rated on the Enhanced Fujita scale, and most of them in the United States occur in a region of the Great Plains known as an "Alley." For 10 points, name this storm, also called a twister.

This instrument records the shaking of the ground during an earthquake. It has a heavy mass that stays still while the frame moves with the ground, and it produces a trace called a seismogram. For 10 points, name this device that detects seismic waves.

This is the name of the molten rock beneath Earth's surface. It collects in chambers under volcanoes and forms igneous rocks such as granite when it cools slowly. When it erupts onto the surface it is instead called lava. For 10 points, name this hot liquid rock.

Water that falls from clouds to Earth as rain, snow, sleet, or hail is called this. It is the part of the water cycle that follows condensation. Meteorologists measure it with a rain gauge. For 10 points, name this term for water falling from the sky.

This was the single global ocean that surrounded the supercontinent Pangaea. Its name comes from Greek words meaning "all sea." The Pacific Ocean is considered its remnant, along with the Tethys Sea. For 10 points, give this name.

This is the name for the imaginary line at 0 degrees latitude that divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. For 10 points, name this line, which also marks the region of the warmest tropical climates.

These are the huge masses of land ice that cover Antarctica and Greenland. They hold most of Earth's freshwater, and Antarctica's is up to several miles thick. Their melting would raise sea level. For 10 points, name these continental-scale glaciers.
This is the name for the tiny pieces of rock and mineral, such as sand and silt, that are moved by wind and water and deposited. For 10 points, name this material that forms sedimentary rock.

This is the day on which the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most toward the Sun, giving it the longest daylight of the year. It falls around June 21. The Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day then. For 10 points, name this day that marks the start of astronomical summer.

q: This law states that the force exerted by a spring is proportional to how far it is stretched or compressed from its rest length. It is usually written F equals negative k x. It is named for a seventeenth-century English scientist who also coined the biological term "cell." For 10 points, name this law of elasticity.

This net force acts on an object moving in a circle and is directed toward the center of the circle. It equals mass times velocity squared divided by radius. Gravity supplies it for planets orbiting the Sun, and tension supplies it for a ball whirled on a string. For 10 points, name this force, whose name means "center-seeking."

A falling skydiver speeds up until air drag balances weight, after which the skydiver falls at this constant speed. Opening a parachute increases drag and lowers this speed. It depends on mass, shape, and the density of the fluid. For 10 points, name this maximum steady speed of a falling object.

This quantity is the product of a force and the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force. A longer wrench handle gives more of it for the same force. It is the rotational analog of force and is measured in newton-meters. For 10 points, name this quantity.

This quantity equals the force on an object multiplied by the time over which the force acts. It equals the change in the object's momentum. Airbags and crumple zones reduce the force of a crash by increasing the time of a collision. For 10 points, name this quantity.

This law says that the electric force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. A French engineer measured it in 1785 using a torsion balance. Its form resembles Newton's law of gravitation. For 10 points, name this law of electrostatics.

This circuit component stores energy in an electric field between two conducting plates separated by an insulator. Its capacity is measured in farads. A camera's flash relies on one to release energy quickly. For 10 points, name this component, whose name refers to its capacity to hold charge.

For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, this law says that pressure is inversely proportional to volume. It was published in 1662 by an Anglo-Irish natural philosopher and chemist. A scuba diver's lungs expand as the diver rises because of it. For 10 points, name this gas law.

Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained this process after Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann detected it in 1938. In it, a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and splits, releasing energy and more neutrons. A chain reaction of it powers nuclear reactors. For 10 points, name this process.

This law relates the angles of incidence and refraction to the indices of refraction of two media. It states that the index of the first medium times the sine of its angle equals the index of the second times the sine of its angle. A Dutch astronomer is credited with it in the West. For 10 points, name this law of refraction.

This principle states that where the speed of a moving fluid increases, its pressure decreases. It helps explain lift on an airplane wing and how a perfume atomizer draws liquid upward. A Swiss mathematician published it in his 1738 book Hydrodynamica. For 10 points, name this principle.

This is the spreading of waves as they pass through an opening or around an obstacle. It is most noticeable when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the opening. It lets you hear someone talking around a corner but not see them. For 10 points, name this wave phenomenon, which produces a pattern of bright and dark bands for light passing through a narrow slit.

This phenomenon occurs when a periodic driving force matches the natural frequency of a system, causing the amplitude to grow large. Pushing a child on a swing at the right rhythm demonstrates it. A singer can shatter a wine glass by producing sound at the glass's own frequency, using it. For 10 points, name this effect.

This kind of wave is formed when two waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions and interfere. It has fixed points of zero displacement called nodes and points of maximum displacement called antinodes. A vibrating guitar string is an example. For 10 points, name this kind of wave that does not appear to travel.

This quantity is a measure of disorder, or of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with a system's macroscopic state. The second law of thermodynamics says that the total of it in an isolated system never decreases. Rudolf Clausius coined its name. For 10 points, name this thermodynamic quantity, measured in joules per kelvin.

This quantity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one kelvin. Water has an unusually high value of about 4,200 joules per kilogram-kelvin, which moderates coastal climates. For 10 points, name this property, which is lower for metals than for water.

This is the time required for half the nuclei in a radioactive sample to decay. For carbon-14, it is about 5,730 years, which makes it useful for dating organic remains. It is independent of the sample's initial size. For 10 points, name this quantity.

This law states that the direction of an induced current is such that its magnetic effect opposes the change in flux that produced it. It explains the minus sign in Faraday's law and is a consequence of conservation of energy. For 10 points, name this law, named for a Baltic German physicist who worked in Russia.

This Scottish physicist unified electricity and magnetism with four equations. He predicted that light is an electromagnetic wave. He also helped develop the kinetic theory of gases and produced an early color photograph in 1861. For 10 points, name this physicist, for whom the equations are named.

In this phenomenon, light shining on a metal surface ejects electrons only if the light's frequency exceeds a threshold, no matter how bright it is. Heinrich Hertz first observed it, and Einstein explained it in 1905 using light quanta. For 10 points, name this effect that won Einstein his Nobel Prize.

This phenomenon occurs when light traveling in a denser medium strikes a boundary with a less dense medium at an angle beyond the critical angle. No light is transmitted and all of it is reflected. It keeps light trapped inside optical fibers and makes diamonds sparkle. For 10 points, name this effect.

This property of transverse waves describes the orientation of the oscillations. Sunglasses with lenses that block horizontally oriented light reduce glare from roads and water. It demonstrates that light is a transverse wave rather than a longitudinal one. For 10 points, name this property of light.

In 1798, this English scientist used a torsion balance with lead spheres to measure the density of the Earth, an experiment later interpreted as determining the gravitational constant. He also discovered hydrogen, which he called "inflammable air." He was famously shy. For 10 points, name this scientist, for whom a laboratory at Cambridge is named.
